issues.legal_issue: A tenant parts with possession only when the tenant transfers legal possession of the premises or a part of them, excluding the tenant, rather than merely allowing a third party to use a display board while the tenant retains possession and uses the premises for the tenant’s own business.
material_facts: The tenant operated an optical business and also carried on an advertising business, maintaining display boards at various locations.
The tenant installed and maintained a board on the roof area and charged for advertising, including amounts for painting and other expenses.

The tenant testified that the roof had not been given to anyone and that the tenant retained possession; the evidence did not establish that the advertiser had exclusive possession or a right to exclude the tenant.
The landlord’s letter from the advertising company stating that it had the site was written after the eviction suit had been filed, and the landlord did not submit to cross-examination after remand.
The other asserted grounds did not support eviction: no default warranting eviction was found, and the appellate court had rejected material alteration.
issues.conclusion: The display board and receipt of advertising charges did not establish an assignment, subletting, or parting with possession under section 13(1)(e). The eviction order could not stand, and the appeal was allowed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(1)(e) of the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950 requires an assignment, subletting, or other parting with possession of the whole or part of the premises without the landlord’s permission. Subletting requires transfer of an exclusive right to enjoy the property; parting with possession requires transfer of legal possession to the exclusion of the tenant. Mere occupation or use by another, or the tenant’s receipt of money, is insufficient without the requisite transfer. The Court relied on Shalimar Tar Products v. H.C. Sharma, Gundalpalli Rangamannar Chetty v. Desu Rangiah, Jackson v. Simons, Chaplin v. Smith, Vishwa Nath v. Chaman Lal, Madras Bangalore Transport Co. v. Inder Singh, Dr. Vijay Kumar v. M/s. Raghbir Singh Anokh Singh, B.M. Lal v. Dunlop Rubber & Co., Rajbir Kaur v. M/s. S. Chokosiri and Co., Dipak Banerjee v. Lilabati Chakroborty, Associated Hotel of India Ltd. v. S.B. Sardar Ranjit Singh, and Krishnawati v. Hans Raj. The inquiry depends on the quality of the occupation and whether the tenant retained legal possession and control.

rule.if: eviction_proceeding_on_transfer_ground and tenant_retained_legal_possession and advertiser_lacked_exclusive_possession and tenant_used_premises_for_own_business

predicates.eviction_proceeding_on_transfer_ground: The proceeding sought eviction on the basis that the tenant had assigned, sublet, or otherwise parted with possession of the premises or part of them.
predicates.tenant_retained_legal_possession: The tenant remained in legal possession and control of the area used for the display board.
predicates.advertiser_lacked_exclusive_possession: The advertiser was not shown to have an exclusive right to possess the area or to exclude the tenant from it.
predicates.tenant_used_premises_for_own_business: The tenant used the premises or the display board in carrying on the tenant’s own business.

issues.definition: When an eviction proceeding rests on a transfer ground, the tenant’s retained legal possession, the advertiser’s lack of exclusive possession, and the tenant’s own business use mean that the transfer ground does not support eviction.

issues.legal_issue: A witness’s examination-in-chief that is not followed by cross-examination after the court has directed the witness to appear for it is unsafe to rely on as proof of the witness’s allegations.
material_facts: The landlord gave evidence in examination-in-chief before the case was remanded.
The case was remanded because the tenant had not been allowed to cross-examine the landlord or present defence evidence.
After remand, the court directed the landlord to appear for cross-examination, but the landlord did not do so despite several opportunities.
The landlord did not otherwise produce evidence supporting the allegations that the tenant had parted with possession.
issues.conclusion: It was unsafe to rely on the landlord’s untested examination-in-chief, and the landlord’s allegations of parting with possession were not established by that testimony. Cross-examination could not be used to go beyond the examination-in-chief to create a case that had not been made in that evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 137 and 138 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 govern examination-in-chief and cross-examination. A party is not to be given an opportunity through cross-examination to make out a case beyond the evidence given in examination-in-chief; where the witness does not submit to cross-examination after an order requiring it, reliance on the untested examination-in-chief is unsafe in the circumstances described by the Court.

predicates.civil_trial_after_remand: The case was tried again after a court remanded it for further proceedings.
predicates.plaintiff_testimony_recorded_in_chief: The plaintiff gave testimony in examination-in-chief.
predicates.plaintiff_did_not_submit_to_cross_examin: After being directed to appear for cross-examination, the plaintiff did not submit to it.

issues.definition: When a civil trial resumes after remand, a plaintiff’s examination-in-chief that remains untested because the plaintiff does not submit to cross-examination is unsafe to rely on.
